description: General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679). Applies since 25 May 2018. Establishes rights of data subjects and obligations of controllers and processors for personal data. Extra-territorial scope (Art.3). Maximum fines: €20M or 4% global annual turnover for serious infringements.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence. World's first comprehensive AI regulation. Risk-based approach: unacceptable risk (prohibited), high-risk, limited risk, minimal risk. Applies to providers, deployers, importers and distributors. GPAI model obligations from August 2025. High-risk AI requirements from August 2026.

Seven core principles: (1) Lawfulness, fairness, transparency; (2) Purpose limitation; (3) Data minimisation; (4) Accuracy; (5) Storage limitation; (6) Integrity and confidentiality (security); (7) Accountability. Controller must be able to demonstrate compliance (accountability principle).

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 5: "Personal data shall be: (a) processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’);"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Processing is lawful only if at least one basis applies: (a) Consent; (b) Contract; (c) Legal obligation; (d) Vital interests; (e) Public task; (f) Legitimate interests (not applicable to public authorities). For AML/KYC processing: typically Art.6(1)(c) legal obligation and Art.6(1)(f) legitimate interests.

metadata.aml_relevance: Art.6(1)(c) covers AMLR/CDD obligations; Art.6(1)(f) for fraud prevention

canonical_name: GDPR Article 6 — Lawful Bases for Processing

description: Processing of racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, genetic/biometric data, health data, sex life/sexual orientation data is prohibited unless specific conditions apply. Relevant for PEP screening (political opinions), biometric identity verification, and health data in insurance AML.

metadata.aml_relevance: PEP screening may involve political opinions data
metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 9: "Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited. 2."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — extracted verbatim from the Official Journal text

canonical_name: GDPR Article 9 — Special Categories of Data

description: When personal data is collected directly from the data subject, controller must provide: identity/contact details, DPO contact, purposes and legal basis, legitimate interests (if applicable), recipients, transfers, retention period, data subject rights, right to withdraw consent, right to lodge complaint.

Data subjects have the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') when: data no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, data unlawfully processed, legal obligation requires erasure. Does NOT apply when processing necessary for legal obligation (Art.17(3)(b)) — relevant for AML record retention requirements.

metadata.aml_conflict: AML 5-year record retention overrides erasure requests
metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 17: "Paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to the extent that processing is necessary: (a) for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information;"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Data subjects have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects. Exceptions: necessity for contract, legal authorisation, explicit consent. Where allowed, controller must implement safeguards: human oversight, right to contest, express point of view. Relevant for AI-based transaction monitoring and credit scoring.

metadata.ai_relevance: Intersects with EU AI Act high-risk AI classification for credit scoring and fraud detection
metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 22: "The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. 2."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Controllers must implement data protection by design (technical and organisational measures at design stage) and by default (only minimum necessary data processed by default). Relevant for AML system development and AI system deployment.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 25: "The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — extracted verbatim from the Official Journal text

canonical_name: GDPR Article 25 — Data Protection by Design and Default

description: Processing by a processor must be governed by a Data Processing Agreement (DPA). DPA must specify: subject matter, duration, nature and purpose, type of personal data, categories of data subjects, controller's obligations and rights. Mandatory clauses specified in Art.28(3).

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 28: "Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, that is binding on the processor with regard to the controller and that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the controller."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — extracted verbatim from the Official Journal text

description: Controllers with ≥250 employees (or high-risk processing) must maintain records of processing activities (ROPA). ROPA must include: controller identity, purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention periods, security measures.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 30: "Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative, shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: GDPR Article 30 — Records of Processing Activities (ROPA)

description: Controllers and processors must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures (TOMs) to ensure security appropriate to risk. Measures include: pseudonymisation, encryption, resilience, backup and recovery, regular testing. Risk-based approach. Overlaps with DORA ICT security requirements for financial entities.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 32: "In assessing the appropriate level of security account shall be taken in particular of the risks that are presented by processing, in particular from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed. 3."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Controllers must notify supervisory authority of personal data breach within 72 hours unless breach unlikely to result in risk. Notification must include: nature of breach, categories/numbers of data subjects, contact details, likely consequences, measures taken/proposed.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 33: "In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: GDPR Article 33 — Data Breach Notification to Authority

description: DPIA required when processing likely results in high risk. Mandatory for: systematic and extensive profiling, large-scale special categories processing, systematic public monitoring. DPIA must include: description, necessity assessment, risk assessment, measures. Consult DPO before conducting.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 35: "Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies, and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: GDPR Article 35 — Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)

description: DPO is mandatory for: public authorities, large-scale systematic monitoring, large-scale special categories processing. Financial institutions typically required to appoint DPO. DPO must be expert in data protection law and practice. Must have resources, access to senior management, and independence.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 37: "The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where: (a) the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity;"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Transfers to third countries without adequacy decision require appropriate safeguards: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs), approved codes of conduct/certification schemes. Relevant for cross-border AML data sharing with non-EU FIUs and correspondent banking.

metadata.aml_relevance: Cross-border SAR sharing and FIU data exchanges

canonical_name: GDPR Article 46 — Transfers to Third Countries

description: Member States may provide exemptions from certain GDPR provisions for processing for journalistic, academic, artistic or literary purposes where necessary to reconcile privacy with freedom of expression.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art. 85: "Member States shall by law reconcile the right to the protection of personal data pursuant to this Regulation with the right to freedom of expression and information, including processing for journalistic purposes and the purposes of academic, artistic or literary expression."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — extracted verbatim from the Official Journal text

canonical_name: GDPR Article 85 — Processing for Journalistic/Academic/Research Purposes

description: Prohibited AI systems include: subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring by public authorities, real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces (with narrow exceptions), AI inferring emotions in workplace/education, biometric categorisation revealing sensitive attributes, and predictive policing based on profiling.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 5: "The following AI practices shall be prohibited:"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: AI Act Article 5 — Prohibited AI Practices

description: AI systems are high-risk if they: (a) are a safety component of a product covered by sectoral legislation (Annex I) and require third-party conformity assessment; or (b) are listed in Annex III (standalone high-risk AI areas). Deployers may reclassify as not high-risk if significant safety risk is demonstrably absent.
canonical_name: AI Act Article 6 — Classification as High-Risk AI

description: High-risk AI providers must establish, implement and maintain a risk management system throughout the AI system lifecycle. Must identify and analyse known and foreseeable risks, estimate and evaluate risks, adopt risk mitigation measures, test residual risk. Iterative process throughout development.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 9: "A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems. 2."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: AI Act Article 9 — Risk Management System

description: High-risk AI training, validation and testing data must meet quality criteria: relevant, representative, free from errors, complete. Data governance practices required: examination for biases, data gaps, protection of special categories. Documentation of data sources, collection, processing and preparation.

Providers of high-risk AI must draw up technical documentation before placing on market. Must include: system description, design, development process, risk management, testing, conformity assessment. Documentation must be maintained and updated. Annex IV specifies required content.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 11: "The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed with sufficient transparency to enable deployers to interpret output and use appropriately. Must include automatic logging (logs) of operations throughout lifetime. Instructions for use (IFU) must be provided to deployers.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 13: "High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — extracted verbatim from the Official Journal text

description: High-risk AI systems must enable effective human oversight. Deployers must assign qualified humans who can monitor the AI, intervene or interrupt, understand AI capabilities and limitations, and not follow biased or erroneous AI outputs. Human oversight measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 14: "High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. 2."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Deployers of high-risk AI must: use AI per instructions for use; assign human oversight to qualified persons; monitor AI operation; notify provider/authority of incidents; conduct fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) for public body deployers or regulated private bodies. Perform DPIA under GDPR if applicable.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 26: "Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems, pursuant to paragraphs 3 and 6."
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: AI Act Article 26 — Obligations of Deployers

description: High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessment before market placement. Most high-risk AI: internal conformity assessment by provider. Biometric and critical infrastructure AI: third-party assessment by notified body. CE marking and EU declaration of conformity required.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 43: "In demonstrating the compliance of a high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2, the provider shall follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII where: (a) harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 do not exist, and common specifications referred to in Article 41 are not available;"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

description: Providers and deployers (public bodies) must register high-risk AI systems in EU database before market placement or putting into service. GPAI models with systemic risk also registered. Database publicly accessible.
canonical_name: AI Act Article 51 — Registration of High-Risk AI

description: General-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers must: draw up technical documentation, make information available to downstream providers, publish summary of training data, comply with copyright law, develop policy to comply with copyright. Training on publicly available data: only if Copyright Directive exception applies.
canonical_name: AI Act Article 53 — GPAI Model Obligations

description: GPAI models with systemic risk (training compute ≥10^25 FLOPs or designated by Commission) have additional obligations: adversarial testing (red-teaming), incident reporting to Commission within 2 weeks, cybersecurity protection, energy efficiency reporting.

metadata.source_quote: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 55: "In addition to the obligations listed in Articles 53 and 54, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk shall: (a) perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks;"
metadata.source_verified: 2026-08-29 — reference confirmed by article title; quote extracted verbatim

canonical_name: AI Act Article 55 — GPAI Models with Systemic Risk

description: Eight areas of standalone high-risk AI: (1) Biometric ID and categorisation; (2) Critical infrastructure; (3) Education and vocational training; (4) Employment and worker management; (5) Essential private/public services (credit scoring, creditworthiness, life/health insurance risk assessment); (6) Law enforcement; (7) Migration, asylum, border control; (8) Justice and democratic processes.

metadata.aml_relevance: Area 5 includes credit scoring and fraud detection AI used by financial institutions

canonical_name: AI Act Annex III — High-Risk AI Areas

description: Required for high-risk processing under GDPR Art.35. Steps: identify processing type requiring DPIA, describe processing and necessity, assess risks to rights/freedoms, mitigating measures, DPO consultation, supervisory authority prior consultation if high residual risk. Also required when deploying high-risk AI (AI Act Art.26 + GDPR overlap).

Process for handling data subject rights requests under GDPR. Includes: verification of identity, review of applicable processing activities, assess exemptions (e.g. AML record retention, tipping-off prohibition), draft response, meet 30-day deadline (extendable by 2 months for complex cases). AML special rules: SAR response may conflict with tipping-off prohibition.

72-hour breach notification process under GDPR Art.33. Includes: detect and contain breach, assess likelihood and severity of risk, notify supervisory authority (if risk), notify affected data subjects (if high risk, Art.34), document all breaches in breach register. Intersects with DORA Art.18 ICT incident reporting for financial entities.

Natural or legal person who determines the purposes and means of processing personal data (GDPR Art.4(7)). Bears primary GDPR accountability. In financial services: the bank/institution is controller for customer data. Joint controller arrangements arise in data sharing consortia (e.g. financial crime utilities).

Natural or legal person who processes personal data on behalf of a controller (GDPR Art.4(8)). Bound by Data Processing Agreement (Art.28). Must process only on controller's instructions. Common in financial services: cloud providers, KYC screening platforms, AML analytics vendors.

Entity that develops or has an AI system developed and places it on the EU market or puts it into service under its own name/trademark (AI Act Art.3(3)). Providers bear primary AI Act obligations: conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking, registration. Distinction from deployer is crucial for compliance allocation.

Entity that uses an AI system under its authority (AI Act Art.3(4)), except for personal non-professional use. Deployers bear obligations under Art.26: human oversight, FRIA (for public bodies and certain private bodies), monitoring. Financial institutions using third-party AI for credit scoring or AML are deployers.

metadata.financial_relevance: Banks using vendor AML/credit AI are deployers

description: AI model trained on large amounts of data using self-supervision at scale, displaying significant generality and capable of being used for diverse downstream tasks (AI Act Art.3(63)). Examples: large language models (LLMs), foundation models. Subject to Art.53 obligations. Those with systemic risk (≥10^25 FLOPs) also subject to Art.55.

metadata.examples: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama — if placed on EU market

description: AI Act Art.26(9) requires deployers that are public bodies, or private bodies providing public services, or deploying AI in areas of credit scoring and life/health insurance risk assessment, to conduct a FRIA before deploying high-risk AI. FRIA covers: description of deployment, fundamental rights risks, safeguards, role of DPO.

metadata.financial_relevance: Credit scoring AI deployers must conduct FRIA

description: GDPR and AI Act obligations overlap significantly for AI systems processing personal data. Key intersections: (1) DPIA (GDPR Art.35) + FRIA (AI Act Art.26) — may need to be conducted together; (2) Automated decision-making (GDPR Art.22) applies to high-risk AI decisions; (3) Privacy by design (GDPR Art.25) aligns with AI Act Art.10 data governance; (4) Data processor agreements for AI vendors.

Key tensions and overlaps: (1) AML record retention (5 years, AMLR Art.77) vs GDPR storage limitation (Art.5(1)(e)) — resolved by Art.6(1)(c) legal obligation; (2) Tipping-off prohibition prevents full SAR response; (3) PEP screening involves processing of politically sensitive data (GDPR Art.9 borderline); (4) STR/SAR filing is lawful under Art.6(1)(c) and Art.23(1)(d) restriction of rights.

Overlapping incident reporting: ICT incident involving personal data triggers both GDPR Art.33 (72h authority breach notification) and DORA Art.18 (major ICT incident 3-stage reporting). Security measures: GDPR Art.32 TOMs complement DORA Art.9 ICT security controls. DORA threat-intel sharing (Art.45) subject to GDPR constraints on personal data in threat feeds.

AI-based transaction monitoring (TM) systems used for AML may be high-risk AI under Annex III area 5 (fraud detection). AML AI deployers must: assign human oversight (Art.14), conduct FRIA if in scope (Art.26), register system (Art.51). AMLR risk-based approach aligns with AI Act risk management (Art.9). AI-generated SAR narratives raise new accountability questions.

Independent EU body ensuring consistent application of GDPR. Issues binding decisions in cross-border cases, guidelines, recommendations and opinions. Composed of heads of national supervisory authorities (DPAs) and EDPS. Key guidelines: AI (2024), biometrics, legitimate interests (Art.6(1)(f)), consent, international transfers.

metadata.role: GDPR consistency mechanism, guidelines, binding decisions

description: EU body within European Commission responsible for oversight of GPAI models with systemic risk, coordinating AI governance, and developing guidelines under the AI Act. Established within DG CNECT. Lead enforcer for GPAI model obligations.

Supervisory authorities in each Member State responsible for GDPR enforcement. Also act as market surveillance authorities for AI Act enforcement for most high-risk AI. Leading authority in cross-border cases determined by one-stop-shop mechanism (GDPR Art.56). Examples: ICO (UK, post-Brexit), IMY (Sweden), Datatilsynet (Norway/Denmark), Tietosuojavaltuutettu (Finland).

metadata.role: GDPR enforcement, AI Act market surveillance
